description.narrative: The Second Health Systems Development Project aims to assist the Nigerian authorities in redressing the deteriorated delivery of basic health care services, and, to build institutional capacities that would pave the way for a sustained development of the country's health care system. Through its components, the project will: 1) support all states in strengthening the capacity of the State Ministry of Health in the areas of planning, financial management, and monitoring and evaluation, while a limited support will be provided to improve the technical skills of trainers, and key health providers. Support activities will cover managerial processes and skills; technical skill development; improved health management information systems, and, access to information and communication technology, in addition to research and studies; 2) finance, and support activities that improve the delivery of primary health care services, emphasizing on strengthening immunization services, safe motherhood interventions, and communicable disease control (both endemic and epidemic diseases). Access to health care will be improved, as will the availability of essential, and generic drugs in health facilities, in addition to quality of training in nursing, mid-wife services, and health technology schools; and, 3) support capacity building, and strengthening of public health functions, and processes at the Federal Ministry of Health, and, coordinate, monitor and evaluate the implementation of the project. Support for the formulation of health policy, and strategies, the health reform process, and for strengthened management information systems will be financed.

The overriding goal of this project is to assist the Nigerian Health authorities in their efforts to redress the serious deterioration in the delivery of basic health care services following decades of neglect and build institutional capacities, paving the way for a more sustained development of the Nigerian health care system. More specifically, the project would: (i) strengthen capacities for system management at the state level and encourage an environment of broad based consultation; (ii) support improvements in the delivery of primary health care services with a particular focus on maternal and child health and reproductive health services; and (iii) assist the Federal Government to strengthen its policy formulation and further develop a system to monitor the health sector performance.

Progress has been made. 284% overall increase in the number of children who engaged the PHC system to receive the third dose ofDPT3 (48,101 in 2004 to 184,581 in 2011).

actual.value: 53.5% (NICS 2006) 42.2% (NDHS 2008) 67.7%(NICS 2010) Data only collected mainly during surveys (e.g NICS, NDHS etc).

comment.narrative: Routine data difficult to track for this indicator as HMIS does not capture data as presented. Similar data for DPT3 from theproject health facilities showed a steady increase over the life of the project, with an overall increase in the number of childrenwho engaged the PHC system to receive the third dose of DPT3 of 284% (48,101 in 2004 to 184,581 in 2011). The NICS conducted in2003, 2006 and 2010 corroborated this trend with reported coverage of 36.3%, 53.5% and 67.7% across the country respectively.However it should be noted that the DHS results (12.9% in 2003 and 22.7% in 2008) suggest much less progress on immunizationcoverage in the country.

No baseline data included at design. New smear positive cases detected nationwide is reported above for 2004 from the National TBProgram data.
No target set at design

Data available on this indicator is grossly under reported with only three (3) states able to report trend data over the life ofthe project in the data review exercise. However efforts were made to obtain data from the National TB Program (NTP) whichindicated that new smear positive cases detected has increased from 33,755 in 2004 to 47, 436 in 2011 (an increase of about41%). Presentlythe calculation of case detection rate (CDR) for smear positive TB cases has been discontinued by WHO since 2010.However in previously reported data by the NTP, case detection rate for the country rose from 26% in 2004 to about 30.5% in 2008.In 2009, the CDR experienced a decline to 28.9%, a decline attributed to the stock out of anti-TB drugs in the country at thetime.

title.narrative: Percentage of pregnant women attending antenatal clinics (New - added for the additional financing)

comment.narrative: Source of baseline not verifiable, therefore other verifiable data at time of AF design will be used instead 63.4% (NARHS 2007)and57.7% (NDHS 2008)

Source of target set at time of AF design is not verifiable. Progress has been assessed from HMIS and facility data and this hasshown a 553% increase in ANC attendance in numbers, percentages not available.

actual.value: 227,246 (2011 attendance) 1,01,814 (cumulative total attendance) in the 321 project facilities only.

comment.narrative: A steady increase noticed for ANC attendance in the project facilities across the reporting period until 2010 and a declinenoticedin 2011 (this may be due to incomplete reporting from the States at the time of data collection). However, the denominatorfor computing the percentage increase over the life of the project was not established at baseline making it difficult toaccurately estimatethe final result on this indicator. There are two major areas of limitation regarding this, (i) at least 4 ANCvisits for each pregnant women should have been tracked in line with international standards, and (ii) the denominator which isgenerated through population estimate of the number of pregnant women giving birth in the last 12 months should also have beenestablished at baseline. However, the continued increase in ANC visits as reported in the facilities (34,782 in 2004 and 227,246 in2011) coupled with the increase in number of births attended by trained/skilled health personnel shows that the project achievedsome success.
